articles.title: Five ways real MCP clients broke our server
articles.excerpt: An agent once told one of our users that our MCP tools "cannot create projects" and asked them to make four projects by hand. The tools could. The sentence saying so had been cut off before the agent…
articles.body: An agent once told one of our users that our MCP tools "cannot create projects" and asked them to make four projects by hand. The tools could. The sentence saying so had been cut off before the agent ever saw it. That was the fourth way real clients broke our server. I build StateLode, a hosted task board that coding agents read and write over MCP. The server is small: three tools behind one Streamable HTTP endpoint, stateless, a fresh server and transport per request. It passed every test we wrote. The first two bugs below showed up within a week of the endpoint going live; the rest over the next two months. None of them are exotic. If you put an MCP server on the internet, you'll probably hit at least two. 1.

articles.title: Foreman Personal Access Tokens Inherit Broad Default Roles
articles.excerpt: Foreman Personal Access Tokens Inherit Broad Default Roles Foreman administrators manage hosts, organizations, locations, and provisioning workflows. Personal access tokens provide API access without…
articles.body: Foreman Personal Access Tokens Inherit Broad Default Roles Foreman administrators manage hosts, organizations, locations, and provisioning workflows. Personal access tokens provide API access without an interactive password. The token's authority comes from the user's roles and permission filters. A review that checks only token expiry can miss a default role that applies to every user in the system. Start with the role graph Foreman documentation defines roles as sets of permissions and permission filters. It notes that the Default role applies to every user and warns that adding a permission to that role grants it to all users. Inventory predefined and custom roles, their permission filters, and the users or groups assigned to them.

articles.title: Why 'Choose a unique column name.' Depends on Your Locale: The Data Studio's Column-Name Rule
articles.excerpt: I work on OnePassApps, so this is a measurement of our own build, read out of the code we ship. A reader of my post on duplicate CSV headers asked me a fair question and then kept asking it, in a very…
articles.body: I work on OnePassApps, so this is a measurement of our own build, read out of the code we ship. A reader of my post on duplicate CSV headers asked me a fair question and then kept asking it, in a very long thread, and I answered it 48 times. So this post is the answer, written once, where it can be found. The question was: when the Data Studio refuses a column name with "Choose a unique column name.", what exactly is it comparing? The answer, read out of the bundle I fetched the Data Studio's route over plain HTTPS and walked the JavaScript it loads. The Data Studio's data operations do not run in the page. They run in a Web Worker: /assets/data-operation.worker-nH-m3g4I.js — 54,757 bytes on the wire (54,755 characters; the file carries a byte-order mark).

articles.title: Password Reset Email Timing — Evidence Chains for Student Report Workflows
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: A password reset email is delayed because several independently queued systems must accept, process, and deliver it. Treat the message as an asynchronous security event: record when the request…
articles.body: TL;DR: A password reset email is delayed because several independently queued systems must accept, process, and deliver it. Treat the message as an asynchronous security event: record when the request was accepted, when an SMTP handoff succeeded or failed, and when the reset token expires. For an edtech system that also emails a generated student report, retain those events separately from the report itself. The least complex design is a durable job record, a bounded retry policy, and an audit record that can explain the timeline without retaining more student data than the investigation requires. What is the bill actually made of? The visible action is one click.

articles.title: How many tokens does an MCP server cost, and how to cut it
articles.excerpt: Originally published at taskhold.com. Short answer: Ask the server for tools/list and divide the JSON's length by four for an estimate, or paste it into Taskhold's free MCP token counter. Input schema…
articles.body: Originally published at taskhold.com . Short answer: Ask the server for tools/list and divide the JSON's length by four for an estimate, or paste it into Taskhold's free MCP token counter. Input schemas and long descriptions make up most of it, and the easiest cut is repeated boilerplate such as the regex zod's .uuid() writes into every id field. Removing that regex took Taskhold's own list from about 8,000 tokens to about 7,200 without changing a description. An MCP server's tool names, descriptions and input schemas are text the model has to read. Connect a few servers and that text can take a real share of the context window before the agent does any work.

articles.title: What a Claude Code plugin runs before you type: we read 2,688 public plugins
articles.excerpt: Before you install a Claude Code plugin, open three things in its folder: hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json and bin/. Look for SessionStart hooks, and for MCP servers started with npx or uvx but no version…
articles.body: Before you install a Claude Code plugin, open three things in its folder: hooks/hooks.json , .mcp.json and bin/ . Look for SessionStart hooks, and for MCP servers started with npx or uvx but no version number. The reason is simple. A plugin can run code before you type anything. The docs say it directly: "A Claude Code plugin you install can execute arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges." Four parts of a plugin start on their own: SessionStart hooks run shell commands when a session starts. Their plain-text output is added to Claude's context, which Claude "can see and act on". MCP servers declared with a command are processes Claude Code starts on your machine for an enabled plugin.

articles.title: RAG vs fine-tuning: which should your LLM app use?
articles.excerpt: Use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) when your app needs facts that change or answers you must cite, and fine-tuning when the model must behave differently, such as a strict format or tone. Nodus…
articles.body: Use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) when your app needs facts that change or answers you must cite, and fine-tuning when the model must behave differently, such as a strict format or tone. Nodus runs both halves: an OpenAI-compatible inference API with embeddings for the retrieval side, and LoRA fine-tuning jobs where a small 8B run costs an estimated $1.54 of GPU time at list prices. Many production apps end up using both, with a fine-tuned model reading retrieved documents. What is the actual difference between RAG and fine-tuning? RAG changes what the model reads; fine-tuning changes the model itself. With RAG, your app searches a document index at request time and pastes the best passages into the prompt.

articles.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
articles.excerpt: Certain configurations of Alpine are affected. Other distros may be as well.
articles.body: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password. The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.

articles.body: Blue Origin's big rocket is getting a little bigger. The stage, called the GS3, "enhances New Glenn's capabilities," Blue Origin said in a blog post today . "The third stage enables direct deployment of satellite constellations to GEO [ geostationary orbit ] and supports heavy-lift science and exploration missions to the moon and deep space." Illustration of the variants of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, with the new GS3 third stage now in the mix. (Image credit: Blue Origin) New Glenn is a two-stage vehicle at the moment.

articles.title: Earth has captured a new mini moon  — but it won't stick around for long
articles.excerpt: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and QQ8 is sticking around for Christmas.
articles.body: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and it is sticking around for Christmas. The space rock, designated 2026 QQ8, was first observed in August 2026 after entering orbit around Earth in April 2026. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on Thursday (Oct. 29). The stay of QQ8 is a temporary one. The mini-moon will remain in the thrall of Earth's gravity through December before breaking away in 2027. Scientists have recreated the orbital path of QQ8, finding that it takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year, to orbit the sun . QQ8 closely approaches Earth around once every ten years, but this time the object came so close that Earth has been able to gravitationally seize it.
